entities.name: credit assignment
entities.definition: Any process for evaluating ('assigning credit' to) the effects of individual actions on solving a problem; the general problem of intelligence that frames the course.

entities.name: generate-and-test
entities.definition: The shared structure of individual learning actions: a goal-directed agent generates actions, tests their effects on goals through trial-and-error feedback, and modifies actions accordingly.

entities.name: intermediate feedback
entities.definition: Proxies evaluated during a task (not only at its end) that indicate progress toward a goal; Samuel's general shape of a credit-assignment solution (e.g., counting checkers pieces).

entities.name: combinatorial explosion
entities.definition: The combinatorial increase in the cost of trial-and-error learning produced by a merely linear increase in interdependent actions; it overwhelms reinforcement policies.

entities.name: superstitious learning
entities.definition: Reinforcing beliefs about actions without enough intermediate feedback to tell whether they are true or merely correlated.

entities.name: reinforcement learning
entities.definition: A paradigm that assigns credit by 'reinforcing' actions that seem to move closer to a goal — increasing their probability of being generated — with the overall goal of maximizing rewards.

entities.name: society of mind
entities.definition: Minsky's paradigm: intelligence as learning to assign credit within a 'society' of many specialized agents that coordinate and cooperate, rather than by maximizing a single reward.

entities.name: policy
entities.definition: In reinforcement learning, the set of rules defining how to update the probabilities ('beliefs') of generating actions as feedback accumulates.

entities.name: learning rate
entities.definition: The policy parameter (0-1) setting how much an action's generation probability is updated per trial; low values are exploitative, high values explorative.

entities.name: reward
entities.definition: An effect of an action on a goal; the scalar quantity reinforcement learning seeks to maximize.

entities.name: exploration-exploitation tradeoff
entities.definition: The tradeoff between a low learning rate (exploits prior feedback — effective but inefficient) and a high learning rate (explores — efficient but risks converging on the wrong beliefs).

entities.name: temporal differencing
entities.definition: Sutton & Barto's reinforcement method that addresses combinatorial explosion by assigning credit to a value function estimating cumulative expected reward — using the time difference between successive predictions — instead of to interdependent actions.

entities.name: reward hypothesis
entities.definition: Sutton & Barto's claim that all of what we mean by goals and purposes can be cast as maximizing the expected value of a cumulative scalar reward signal.

entities.name: management hypothesis
entities.definition: The course's name for Minsky's view that goals and purposes are managed by decomposing problems and memories into societies of agents and assigning credit within them to satisfy higher-level evaluative functions.

entities.name: society of agents
entities.definition: A decomposition of a problem into many specialized agents (e.g., Builder, Add, Grasp, Move) whose coordinated configuration — not any individual agent's reward — is what gets reinforced.

entities.name: Arthur Samuel
entities.definition: IBM scientist whose 1959 checkers program introduced intermediate feedback and the reinforcement shape of credit-assignment solutions.

entities.name: Marvin Minsky
entities.definition: Co-founder of the MIT AI Lab; argued reinforcement cannot generally solve credit assignment and proposed learning in a 'society of mind'.

entities.name: Richard Sutton
entities.definition: With Andrew Barto, developed temporal differencing and articulated the reward hypothesis as a general solution to credit assignment.

entities.name: T-maze
entities.definition: A simplest-case maze used twice in the notes: a mouse navigating it to find cheese (reinforcement) and 'Geoffrey' constructing it from blocks (society of agents).

claims.proposition: Credit assignment is any process for evaluating the effects of individual actions on solving a problem.
A linear increase in the number of interdependent actions produces a combinatorial increase in the cost of trial-and-error learning, which overwhelms reinforcement policies.
Reinforcing beliefs about actions without enough intermediate feedback to assign credit produces superstitious learning.
claims.conditions: feedback about interdependent actions is delayed or ambiguous

claims.proposition: In reinforcement learning, credit is assigned by increasing the probability of generating actions that lead to rewards, governed by a policy whose learning rate sets how much each belief is updated per trial.

A low learning rate (exploitation) assigns credit conservatively but needs inefficiently many trials, while a high learning rate (exploration) updates rapidly but risks converging on the wrong beliefs — the exploration-exploitation tradeoff.
claims.conditions: feedback is costly, so policies must be efficient as well as effective

claims.proposition: All of what we mean by goals and purposes can be well thought of as the maximization of the expected value of the cumulative sum of a received scalar signal (reward).
claims.conditions: claimed to hold for any problem requiring intelligence

claims.proposition: Temporal differencing addresses combinatorial explosion by assigning credit to a value function estimating cumulative reward, rather than to beliefs about interdependent actions.

Feedback is not merely ambiguous but sparse — only a small subset of actions generate feedback useful for assigning credit — so credit assignment is about understanding problems, not maximizing rewards.
claims.conditions: problems for which most possible actions yield no useful feedback

claims.proposition: All of what we mean by goals and purposes can be well thought of as managing processes of decomposing problems, and memories about them, into societies of agents, and assigning credit within these societies so they satisfy higher-level evaluative functions.
claims.conditions: claimed as the general view of credit assignment

claims.proposition: Learning in a society to construct two T-mazes adds little to the credit-assignment challenge, because the same society of agents constructs both — unlike trial-and-error learning, which explodes combinatorially.
claims.conditions: the added actions are the same kind already mastered

tensions.dimension: the nature of goals and the source of intelligence: maximizing a single scalar reward vs. managing a problem's decomposition across a society of agents
tensions.conditions_a: The reward hypothesis better describes credit assignment when feedback is dense enough to estimate cumulative value, the problem is fixed and well-defined, and a single scalar reward captures the goal — e.g., games like checkers, or a platform maximizing engagement.
tensions.conditions_b: The management hypothesis better describes credit assignment when feedback is sparse and the problem itself must be understood and decomposed, when goals are emergent properties of the whole (like a maze's 'containment') not reducible to any one agent's reward, and when prior structure must be remembered and reused — e.g., constructing a novel artifact or reformulating a firm's strategy.

probes.prompt: Sutton's reward hypothesis says every goal can be cast as maximizing a cumulative scalar reward. Minsky's management hypothesis says intelligence is about decomposing a problem into a society of agents. Under what conditions does each better describe how credit gets assigned? Give one case where reward-maximization is enough and one where it isn't.
expected_signals: Names dense or well-defined feedback (e.g., a game, an engagement metric) as where reward-maximization suffices.
Names sparse feedback or novel, ill-defined problems as where reward-maximization breaks down.
Recognizes that some goals (e.g., a maze's 'containment') are properties of the whole, not assignable to any single agent's reward.
Notes the management view requires decomposing the problem and remembering/reusing prior structure.
Does NOT declare one hypothesis universally correct — keeps the tension conditional.

probes.prompt: Why does adding a second T-maze make the mouse's credit-assignment problem more than twice as hard? Explain what 'combinatorial explosion' means here and what it implies for trial-and-error learning.
expected_signals: Explains that one added interdependent action multiplies the number of action-paths (the second maze is really two, depending on the first) — a combinatorial, not linear, increase.
Connects this to the cost of trial-and-error feedback growing combinatorially.
States that combinatorial explosion overwhelms reinforcement / trial-and-error policies.
Optionally links it to superstitious learning — reinforcing beliefs without enough feedback to assign credit.
